section.title: Bodily Discharges
section.sectionRationale: This is the last of the purity laws before the Day of Atonement, the seam moving from the extraordinary case of skin disease to the utterly ordinary case of bodily discharges tied to reproduction and death, showing that no corner of daily life falls outside the holiness code.
section.thesis: God requires that Israel's ordinary bodily discharges, tied to reproduction, life, and death, be washed and, when prolonged, atoned for, teaching a people camped around a holy God's tent that even the everyday leakage of mortal life must be kept from defiling His dwelling place among them.
section.frameNote: Five movements: a man's chronic discharge; the temporary uncleanness of an emission of semen; a woman's monthly impurity; a woman's prolonged discharge and its atoning offering; and the closing purpose, keeping Israel separate from uncleanness so they do not defile the tabernacle in their midst.

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
“Say to the Israelites, ‘When any man has a bodily {{zav|discharge}}, the discharge is unclean.
This uncleanness is from his discharge, whether his body allows the discharge to flow or blocks it. So his discharge will bring about uncleanness.
Any bed on which the man with the discharge lies will be unclean, and any furniture on which he sits will be unclean.
Anyone who touches his bed must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Whoever sits on furniture on which the man with the discharge was sitting must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Whoever touches the body of the man with a discharge must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
If the man with the discharge spits on one who is clean, that person must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Any saddle on which the man with the discharge rides will be unclean.
Whoever touches anything that was under him will be unclean until evening, and whoever carries such things must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
If the man with the discharge touches anyone without first rinsing his hands with water, the one who was touched must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Any clay pot that the man with the discharge touches must be broken, and any wooden utensil must be rinsed with water.
When the man has been cleansed from his discharge, he must count off seven days for his cleansing, wash his clothes, and bathe himself in fresh water, and he shall be clean.
On the eighth day he is to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, come before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, and give them to the priest.
The priest is to sacrifice them, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. In this way the priest will make {{kipper|atonement}} for the man before the LORD because of his discharge.
When a man has an emission of semen, he must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Any clothing or leather on which there is an emission of semen must be washed with water, and it will remain unclean until evening.
If a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen, both must bathe with water, and they will remain unclean until evening.
When a woman has a discharge consisting of blood from her body, she will be unclean due to her {{niddah|menstruation}} for seven days, and anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.
Anything on which she lies or sits during her menstruation will be unclean,
and anyone who touches her bed must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
Whoever touches any furniture on which she was sitting must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
And whether it is a bed or furniture on which she was sitting, whoever touches it will be unclean until evening.
If a man lies with her and her menstrual flow touches him, he will be unclean for seven days, and any bed on which he lies will become unclean.

When a woman has a discharge of her blood for many days at a time other than her menstrual period, or if it continues beyond her period, she will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge, just as she is during the days of her menstruation.
Any bed on which she lies or any furniture on which she sits during the days of her discharge will be unclean, like her bed during her menstrual period.
Anyone who touches these things will be unclean; he must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.
When a woman is cleansed of her discharge, she must count off seven days, and after that she will be ceremonially clean.
On the eighth day she is to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons and bring them to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
The priest is to sacrifice one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. In this way the priest will make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.

units.label: Kept separate, so the tabernacle is not defiled

verses.text: You must keep the children of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die by defiling My {{mishkan|tabernacle}}, which is among them.
This is the law of him who has a discharge, of the man who has an emission of semen whereby he is unclean,
of a woman in her menstrual period, of any male or female who has a discharge, and of a man who lies with an unclean woman.’”

zav.gloss: One who has a flow or discharge, from a root meaning to flow or gush. The word carries no moral weight in itself; it is applied here to bodily discharge and elsewhere to the land flowing with milk and honey, taking its meaning entirely from context.

kipper.gloss: To atone, cover, or make amends. Used at the chapter's turning points to close each case of discharge, tying even an ordinary bodily condition, not itself a sin, to the same covering that dealt with moral guilt elsewhere in Leviticus.

niddah.gloss: Menstrual impurity, from a root meaning to exclude or separate. The word later expands in the prophets into a picture of moral defilement, as when Israel's idolatry is likened to a woman's niddah in Ezekiel 36:17.

mishkan.gloss: Dwelling place, tabernacle, from the root shakan, to dwell. The whole chapter's concern is not abstract hygiene but the concrete fact that a holy God actually dwells among an ordinarily unclean people.

basic.context: This chapter regulates ordinary bodily discharges: chronic issues, emissions of semen, monthly periods, and abnormal bleeding. None of these are sins in themselves, but they render a person ceremonially unclean for a time, requiring washing, and in prolonged cases, an offering.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a ceremonial purity law for Israel's camp gathered around the tabernacle, not a claim that bodies or sexuality are shameful, and not a command binding on Christians today. It teaches that even ordinary bodily life, marked by reproduction and mortality, needed careful boundaries around a holy God's presence.
basic.originalLanguages: The Hebrew zav names one with a flow; niddah names a woman's monthly impurity and later becomes a byword for moral defilement. Kipper, atonement, appears at the chapter's turning points, tying bodily uncleanness to the same covering that dealt with sin.
basic.typology: Washing and waiting until evening pictures a cleansing these rituals could only symbolize; an offering brought for a bodily condition that was never itself sin shows that Israel's atonement reached further than moral guilt, anticipating a Savior whose cleansing reaches every corner of human frailty.
basic.christ: Jesus lets a woman with a twelve year discharge of blood touch Him, exactly the person this law separated from the camp, and instead of becoming unclean Himself, He makes her clean, reversing the flow of defilement into a flow of healing, Mark 5:25-34.
basic.god: God is holy and near at once: near enough that ordinary human bodies, in birth, sex, and blood, must be considered in relation to His presence, yet gracious in providing everyday washing, not permanent exclusion, as the remedy.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 5:25-34 and Luke 8:43-48 show Jesus healing the woman with the flow of blood this very law describes. Ezekiel 36:17 uses niddah of Israel's moral impurity. Hebrews 9:13-14 argues from these external washings to the deeper cleansing of the conscience in Christ.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's careful boundaries around ordinary bodily life foreshadow the deeper truth that all human existence, not only visible sin, needs the cleansing God provides. That cleansing culminates when Christ touches the unclean and makes them whole, and is complete in the washing and sanctification believers now have in Him.

context.literary:
Leviticus 15 is arranged as a careful mirror. It opens with a man's abnormal, chronic discharge, verses 2 to 15, then moves to a man's normal emission of semen, verses 16 and 17. At the centre stands verse 18, a man and a woman together in marital intimacy. The chapter then turns to a woman's normal monthly flow, verses 19 to 24, and ends with a woman's abnormal, prolonged bleeding, verses 25 to 30. Chronic male, normal male, the couple, normal female, chronic female: the structure places man and woman on equal footing and puts the one shared act at the hinge.

The two outer cases match closely. Each describes how uncleanness spreads to beds and seats, each requires the healed person to "count off seven days," verses 13 and 28, and each ends on the eighth day with two turtledoves or two young pigeons, a sin offering and a burnt offering, and the words "the priest will make atonement," verses 15 and 30. The inner cases, by contrast, require only washing and waiting "until evening." The law distinguishes clearly between what is prolonged and abnormal and what is ordinary and passing.

A refrain runs through the chapter like a drumbeat: "must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening." It sounds well over a dozen times across the chapter, and the repetition teaches that these are everyday matters with everyday remedies.

Verse 31 then steps back to give the purpose not only of this chapter but of the whole purity block from chapter 11 onward: "You must keep the children of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them." Verses 32 and 33 close with the summary formula. The very next chapter, the Day of Atonement, answers verse 31 directly, when the high priest cleanses the sanctuary "because it is surrounded by their impurities," Leviticus 16:16.
context.historical:
The chapter assumes an ordinary household: beds, seats, saddles, clay pots and wooden bowls, verses 4 to 12. The rules that a clay pot touched by the man with a discharge must be broken while a wooden utensil is rinsed, verse 12, match the rules for dead creatures in Leviticus 11:32-33. Unglazed pottery was porous and could not be reliably cleaned; wood could be rinsed. The law worked with the materials people actually used.

It also limits the spread of uncleanness in practical ways. If the man with a discharge rinses his hands, his touch does not pass uncleanness to others, verse 11. Most secondary contact produced only a one day uncleanness ended by washing. Life could go on in the home.

Leviticus 15 itself describes the person with a discharge living among household furniture. Numbers 5:2-3 commands that those with a discharge be sent outside the wilderness camp, where the LORD dwelt among the tribes. Interpreters differ on whether Numbers applies a stricter rule to the war camp around the tabernacle or describes the same law from another angle.

Many ancient peoples kept menstrual taboos, and some feared the blood as dangerous in itself. Leviticus treats the flow neither as demonic nor as shameful, and it applies the same kind of rules to men's discharges. The concern is always the holy things and the holy place.

The chapter shaped Israel's life for centuries. The narrator notes that Bathsheba "had just purified herself from her uncleanness," 2 Samuel 11:4. Ezekiel lists not approaching "a woman during her period" among the marks of a righteous man, Ezekiel 18:6. By Jesus' day the tradition of washings had grown far beyond the text, to "the washing of cups, pitchers, kettles, and couches for dining," Mark 7:4. The woman of Mark 5 had lived under this law for twelve years and had "spent all she had" on physicians, Mark 5:26.
context.canonical:
The chapter's concern for ritual purity before holy moments echoes across the Old Testament. Before the LORD descends on Sinai, the people are told, "Do not draw near to a woman," Exodus 19:15. Deuteronomy 23:10-11 applies the rule of verse 16 to Israel's war camp, and the priest at Nob will give David's men the consecrated bread only if they "have kept themselves from women," 1 Samuel 21:4. Priests with a discharge could not eat the holy offerings until they were clean, Leviticus 22:4-7.

The prophets turn the vocabulary of verse 19 into a picture of the nation's sin. Ezekiel says Israel's behaviour was "like the uncleanness of a woman's impurity," Ezekiel 36:17. Lamentations says of Jerusalem, "Her uncleanness stains her skirts," Lamentations 1:9, and "Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them," Lamentations 1:17. Isaiah confesses, "Each of us has become like something unclean," Isaiah 64:6. Yet the same prophets promise cleansing: "I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean," Ezekiel 36:25, and Zechariah foresees "a fountain" opened "to cleanse them from sin and impurity," Zechariah 13:1.

The Gospels bring the chapter into a single scene. A woman "who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years," Mark 5:25, the prolonged discharge of Leviticus 15:25, touches Jesus and is healed. Mark sets her story inside the raising of Jairus' daughter, a girl of twelve who has died, Mark 5:42, so that Jesus meets the uncleanness of blood and the uncleanness of death in one journey.

Hebrews then reflects on the whole system of washings. They were "external regulations imposed until the time of reform," Hebrews 9:10, and if they cleansed the body, "how much more will the blood of Christ... purify our consciences," Hebrews 9:13-14. Believers now draw near with "our bodies washed with pure water," Hebrews 10:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author's purpose is stated in the chapter itself: to keep Israel from dying by defiling the tabernacle "which is among them," verse 31. The emphasis falls on the last words. The LORD had chosen to live in the middle of the camp, Exodus 25:8, and that nearness meant that even the most private parts of life had a bearing on the whole community's safety before Him.

The author also meant to teach Israel the difference between the holy and the ordinary in terms they could not forget. Every Israelite, man or woman, would experience the conditions of this chapter. The law ensured that each one regularly remembered that the body, good as it is, is mortal and marked, and that the holy God is not to be approached casually.

He wanted, too, to keep the remedy close at hand. Most cases end with washing and sunset. Even the chronic cases, which need an offering, are met with one of the cheapest sacrifices in the system, two birds, and the same atonement for man and woman alike. The first hearers were meant to live ordinary married and family life without fear, while honouring the boundaries of God's dwelling.

Finally, by placing marital intimacy at the chapter's centre, verse 18, and requiring only washing, the author set sex apart from worship without treating it as sin. In a world where neighbouring religions often entwined fertility and worship, Israel's God kept the two distinct.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescriptive for Israel living around the tabernacle. Its washings, waiting periods and offerings are not binding on Christians. Jesus declared that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile the heart, Mark 7:19, and Paul could write that "nothing is unclean in itself," Romans 14:14. The sanctuary these laws protected has been replaced by Christ Himself and by His people as God's temple, 1 Corinthians 6:19.

Two cautions follow. Christians should not revive the ritual categories of this chapter, treating menstruation, childbirth or marital intimacy as disqualifying believers from prayer, the Lord's Supper or church. Nor should they swing to the opposite error and treat the body as irrelevant to holiness. The New Testament still calls believers to "control his own body in holiness and honor," 1 Thessalonians 4:4, and to keep "the marriage bed" undefiled, Hebrews 13:4.

The moral law against intercourse during menstruation, Leviticus 18:19 and 20:18, sits among the sexual laws rather than among the purity laws, and Christians differ on whether it carries into the new covenant. Leviticus 15 itself describes impurity, not sin, and prescribes cleansing, not punishment.

debates.question: Does this law imply that bodily functions or sexuality are shameful or sinful?

views.label: Ceremonial impurity, not moral sin
views.case: The text never calls the discharge a sin; it is treated much like touching a corpse elsewhere in Leviticus, a ritual state requiring washing, not repentance, before approaching the tabernacle. The man and wife of verse 18 simply bathe, and the chapter's refrain of washing and evening shows how ordinary these states are.

views.label: A deliberate association with mortality
views.case: Others note these are precisely the bodily events most tied to procreation and to the slow ebbing of life, so the law visibly reminds Israel of mortality and the fall every time these ordinary things occur. Blood and seed are the carriers of life, and their loss is a small picture of death.

debates.bearing: Either way, the law does not shame the body or sexuality as such; it marks a boundary between ordinary human life, touched by death's shadow, and the holy God who dwells among them. Scripture elsewhere celebrates married love without embarrassment, Genesis 2:25 and Song of Songs 4:7.

debates.question: Why does Leviticus 15:24 treat a man who lies with a menstruating woman as unclean for seven days, when Leviticus 20:18 says both must be cut off?

views.label: Accidental versus deliberate
views.case: Many interpreters hold that 15:24 describes a case where the flow begins unexpectedly or unknowingly, 'her menstrual flow touches him,' and so only ritual impurity follows, while 20:18 describes a deliberate act, 'he has exposed the source of her flow,' which is treated as a moral offence.

views.label: Two different kinds of law
views.case: Others note that chapter 15 is a purity law describing the effects of contact, while chapters 18 and 20 are moral laws about forbidden sexual relations. The same act can have a ritual consequence in one code and a moral verdict in another.

debates.bearing: The two views largely agree. Leviticus 15 is concerned with the transmission of impurity and its remedy, not with judging the act. The penalty of chapter 20 addresses knowing disregard of the command in Leviticus 18:19.

debates.question: Why do ordinary, healthy functions like menstruation and emission of semen cause uncleanness at all?

views.label: The loss of life fluids pictures death
views.case: Many scholars observe that the purity laws gather around death and its signs: corpses, decaying skin, and here the loss of blood and seed, which carry life. The holy God is the living God, and whatever speaks of death is kept away from Him.

views.label: A separation of sexuality from worship
views.case: Others stress that the chapter keeps the processes of reproduction apart from the sanctuary, guarding Israel against the fertility religion of Canaan, in which sexuality and worship were closely entwined.

views.label: Hygiene and health
views.case: Some point to the practical benefits of washing and separation. The chapter's own stated reason, however, is the tabernacle, verse 31, not health.

debates.bearing: The first two views fit the text best and work together. The chapter does not say these functions are bad; it says the holy God, who is life itself, is not to be approached with the marks of mortality, and that worship is not a place for the processes of human fertility.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb behind zav, "one with a discharge," is zub, to flow. Its other uses are worth noticing. It describes the promised land "flowing with milk and honey," Exodus 3:8, and the water that "gushed out" when God struck the rock, Psalm 78:20. The word is neutral. What flows can be abundance or loss; the context decides.

In verses 2, 3 and 19 the BSB's "body" renders basar, "flesh." In this chapter it is a modest way of referring to the sexual organs, a sense the context makes plain. Verse 3 even distinguishes whether "his body allows the discharge to flow or blocks it," covering both an active flow and an obstruction.

The "emission of semen" of verses 16 to 18 and 32 is literally shikbat zera, "a lying of seed." The noun zera, seed, links the chapter to the birth law, where the woman "produces seed," Leviticus 12:2, and to the great promise of the seed in Genesis 3:15. What is lost in verse 16 is the very stuff of life and of the promise.

Verse 33 describes the menstruating woman with a word from the root dawah, "the one who is unwell in her impurity," the same root used in Leviticus 12:2. It expresses weakness or faintness, not wrongdoing. The chapter's main word for her state, niddah, is later used by the prophets for national defilement, and Zechariah's promise of a fountain "to cleanse them from sin and impurity," Zechariah 13:1, uses niddah for "impurity," joining the two ideas that this chapter keeps apart.

Verse 31's "keep ... separate" is the causative stem of nazar, to set apart. It is the root of nazir, "Nazirite," the one who makes a vow "to separate himself to the LORD," Numbers 6:2. Israel's separation from uncleanness is the flip side of its consecration to God.

The phrase "My tabernacle, which is among them" joins mishkan, dwelling, with betokam, "in their midst." It repeats the language of Exodus 25:8, "so that I may dwell among them." John echoes the same idea when he writes that "the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us," John 1:14, using a Greek verb related to the word for tent.

Finally, "until evening," ad ha'erev, recurs through the chapter. In Israel the day began at sunset, so one day's uncleanness ended with the new day. Leviticus 22:7 makes the logic explicit: "When the sun has set, he will become clean." The remedy for most of these states is simply to wash and wait for God's new day.

typology.type: Washing and waiting until evening, Leviticus 15:5-11 and 15:16-18
typology.fulfillment: The chapter's constant refrain is washing clothes, bathing in water and waiting for the day to end. The washings were real but temporary, 'external regulations imposed until the time of reform,' Hebrews 9:10. In Christ believers receive 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' Titus 3:5, and are told to draw near with 'our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22. The escalation is from the body to the conscience, Hebrews 9:14. The type falls short because the washings had to be repeated every time uncleanness returned; the washing Christ gives makes a person 'completely clean,' John 13:10.

typology.type: The woman with a prolonged flow of blood, Leviticus 15:25-30
typology.fulfillment: Under the law she was unclean 'all the days of her unclean discharge,' and everything she lay or sat on shared her state. The woman of Mark 5:25-34 had lived that way for twelve years. When she touched Jesus, uncleanness did not flow to Him; instead 'power had gone out from Him,' Mark 5:30, and her bleeding stopped. The escalation is that the Holy One's touch cleanses instead of being defiled, and He calls her 'Daughter,' Mark 5:34. The type falls short because the law could only wait for her to heal and then offer atonement; Christ heals her and sends her away in peace.

typology.type: Bathing in living water after seven days, Leviticus 15:13
typology.fulfillment: The man healed of a chronic discharge completes his cleansing in 'fresh water,' literally living water, before his offering on the eighth day. Jesus offers 'living water,' John 4:10, that becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, and promises that 'streams of living water' flow from those who believe, John 7:38. Paul says Christ sanctifies the church, 'cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,' Ephesians 5:26. The escalation is from water that cleanses the skin to the Spirit who renews from within. The type falls short because spring water could not reach the heart.

typology.type: Keeping Israel separate so they do not die by defiling the tabernacle, Leviticus 15:31
typology.fulfillment: The whole purity system existed to protect a dwelling place of God surrounded by a people's uncleanness, and the Day of Atonement cleansed it each year, Leviticus 16:16. Christ, the true high priest, entered 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24, and His people are now the temple in which God dwells, 2 Corinthians 6:16. The escalation is that the danger of death by defilement is removed not by keeping people away, but by making them clean. The type falls short because the tabernacle needed cleansing again every year; Christ's sacrifice is once for all.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most vividly through one woman. Mark introduces her as someone who "had suffered from bleeding for twelve years," Mark 5:25, the prolonged flow of Leviticus 15:25. Under the law everything she touched became unclean, verses 26 and 27, and anyone who touched her bed or seat had to wash and wait. She had spent everything on physicians and grown worse, Mark 5:26. She comes up behind Jesus in the crowd and touches His cloak. Matthew and Luke say she touched the fringe of His cloak, Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44, a word that can refer to the tassels Israelites were commanded to wear on the corners of their garments, Numbers 15:38.

By the logic of Leviticus 15, Jesus should have become unclean until evening. Instead, "Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him," Mark 5:30. The direction of contagion is reversed. Holiness flows out, and impurity is overcome. Jesus then refuses to let her slip away unnoticed. He looks for her, hears her whole story, and calls her "Daughter," Mark 5:34, a public word of acceptance for a woman whom the law had kept at arm's length for twelve years.

Mark frames her story within another. Jesus is on His way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter dies before He arrives. He takes the dead girl by the hand, Mark 5:41, another act that under the law would bring uncleanness, and she rises. The girl is twelve, Mark 5:42, the same number as the years of the woman's suffering. In one journey Jesus meets the two great sources of impurity in Leviticus, the loss of blood and death itself, and overcomes both by touch.

The chapter also leads to Christ by what it cannot do. Its washings dealt with the body; they could not reach the heart. Hebrews argues from lesser to greater: if the ritual waters made bodies clean, "how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death," Hebrews 9:14.

Finally, it leads to Christ as the one in whom God dwells among His people. Leviticus 15:31 guards "My tabernacle, which is among them." In Jesus "the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us," John 1:14. The presence the purity laws protected walked through a crowd and let the unclean touch Him.

A caution belongs here. The details of beds, saddles and clay pots are not symbols of Christ. The link is the one the Gospels make: the one who fulfils the law meets its most persistent uncleanness with healing, and His sacrifice achieves what its washings could only picture.
study.god:
The chapter first shows a God who is not embarrassed by the human body. He speaks plainly about semen, menstruation and abnormal flows, about beds and saddles and spittle. The Creator who made the body male and female, and called it good, is not squeamish about its workings. Holiness in Scripture is not a prudish distance from ordinary life.

Yet He is truly holy, and His holiness is dangerous to those who treat it lightly. Verse 31 speaks of death: Israel could "die by defiling My tabernacle." The living God is the source of life, and what speaks of mortality cannot simply be carried into His presence. The whole chapter trains His people to live near Him with reverence.

He is present. The reason for all these rules is that His dwelling is "among them," verse 31. God did not choose to be worshipped from a distance on a mountaintop alone; He pitched His tent in the middle of the camp, Exodus 25:8. The detailed rules are the price and the proof of that closeness.

He is fair. Man and woman are treated with the same seriousness and the same remedies. The chapter's mirrored structure puts male and female cases side by side, and the chronic cases for both end with the same offering and the same atonement, verses 15 and 30.

He is merciful and practical. Most uncleanness ends with washing and sunset. A man with a discharge who rinses his hands does not pass it on, verse 11. The chronic sufferer is not left in a permanent state but told how to "count off seven days" once healed and to bring one of the least expensive offerings in the system. God's holiness provides its own remedy.

The chapter holds a tension: the body is good, and yet it bears the marks of mortality. God neither denies the goodness nor ignores the mortality. He surrounds ordinary life with reminders of both, and He provides cleansing. In the fullness of time He resolves the tension from His side, dwelling bodily among His people in His Son and promising bodies raised and made new.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to honour God with their bodies, 1 Corinthians 6:19, to approach Him with reverence, and to rejoice that the God who once said "keep separate" now says through Christ, "I will dwell with them and walk among them," 2 Corinthians 6:16.

crossReferences.note: Israel is told to send outside the camp 'anyone who has a bodily discharge' so they will not defile the camp 'where I dwell among them.' The purpose matches Leviticus 15:31 exactly: the presence of God in the midst of the camp is what makes these conditions serious.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest cleanses the sanctuary 'because it is surrounded by their impurities.' This answers the warning of Leviticus 15:31, providing an annual cleansing for the defilement that ordinary uncleanness would otherwise leave on God's dwelling.

A man who becomes unclean through a nocturnal emission must leave the war camp and return after washing at sunset. The rule applies the logic of Leviticus 15:16 to Israel's army, where the LORD moves in the midst of the camp.

The narrator notes that Bathsheba 'had just purified herself from her uncleanness,' the washing that ended menstrual impurity under Leviticus 15:19-24. The detail shows the law practised in ordinary life, and makes clear the child to come was David's.

Israel's defiling of the land is compared to 'the uncleanness of a woman's impurity.' The prophet borrows the language of Leviticus 15:19 to picture moral corruption, and then in verse 25 promises that God will sprinkle clean water and cleanse His people.

A fountain will be opened 'to cleanse them from sin and impurity.' The word for impurity is niddah, the term of Leviticus 15:19. The prophet promises a cleansing that deals with moral sin and ritual defilement together, which the chapter's washings could never do.

A woman with a twelve year flow of blood, the condition of Leviticus 15:25, touches Jesus. Power goes out from Him and she is healed. Jesus calls her 'Daughter' and sends her away in peace, reversing the separation the law imposed on her.

Within the same story Jesus takes the hand of Jairus' dead daughter, aged twelve, and raises her. Together with the healing of the woman, it shows Jesus overcoming the two chief sources of uncleanness, blood and death, by His touch.

The ashes and water that made bodies ceremonially clean are the lesser case; 'how much more' will Christ's blood 'purify our consciences from works of death.' The washings of Leviticus 15 become the starting point of the argument for a deeper cleansing.

Believers draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and 'our bodies washed with pure water.' The language of bathing that runs through Leviticus 15 now describes the confidence with which the cleansed approach God, not the barrier that kept them out.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God made human beings male and female, blessed them, and told them to be fruitful. Their bodies were good, and the man and his wife "were both naked, and they were not ashamed," Genesis 2:25. The fall did not make the body evil, but it brought death into it. Blood and seed, the very carriers of life, became reminders that life now ebbs away.

Leviticus 15 is written for a people who live next to the living God. He has pitched His tent among them, and the question the chapter answers is how mortal bodies, with all their flows and losses, can live beside His holiness without being destroyed. The answer is careful separation, regular washing, and, where the condition persists, atonement. The chapter completes the purity laws of Leviticus 11 to 15 and prepares directly for the Day of Atonement, when the sanctuary itself is cleansed of the impurities that surround it.

The rest of the Old Testament turns the chapter's language into a mirror of the nation's heart. Israel's sin is like a woman's impurity; Jerusalem sits unclean; and the prophets promise clean water, a new heart, and a fountain for sin and impurity.

In Christ the promise is kept. The eternal Word takes flesh and dwells among His people. He lets a bleeding woman touch Him and makes her clean, and He takes a dead girl by the hand and raises her. He offers Himself unblemished to God, so that His blood cleanses not merely bodies but consciences. His people become the temple in which God dwells.

The story ends in a new creation where the tension of this chapter is resolved for good. "The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them," Revelation 21:3. There will be "no more death," Revelation 21:4, and so nothing left that speaks of death. Bodies will be raised imperishable, and the life that once ebbed away will flow unending from the river of the water of life.

quiz.q: What made a man's bodily discharge ceremonially significant in this chapter?

options.text: It rendered him, and anything he touched or sat on, unclean until washed.
options.note: Verses 2-12 spell out this spreading uncleanness in detail.

options.text: It meant he had sinned against God.
options.note: The text never treats the discharge itself as sin, only as a ritual uncleanness.

options.text: It only affected the man himself, not his surroundings.
options.note: Verses 4-12 show the uncleanness spreading to beds, seats, and those who touch him.

options.text: It had no bearing on his daily life at all.
options.note: The whole chapter addresses exactly this concern in careful detail.

quiz.q: What was required on the eighth day after a discharge had ended?

options.text: Two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering.
options.note: Verses 14-15 and 29-30 both specify this offering.

options.text: A single lamb sacrificed at the tabernacle.
options.note: The text specifies two birds, not one lamb.

options.text: Forty days of separation from the camp.
options.note: The period specified is seven days of counting toward cleansing, then an eighth day offering, not forty days.

options.text: No offering was required at all.
options.note: Verses 14-15 explicitly require an offering.

quiz.q: How long was a woman considered unclean during her ordinary monthly period, according to this law?

options.text: Seven days.
options.note: Verse 19 states this directly.

options.text: Until she gave birth.
options.note: That concerns childbirth, addressed in chapter 12, a separate law.

options.text: Forty or eighty days.
options.note: Those figures concern purification after childbirth, not the ordinary monthly period.

options.text: She was never considered unclean.
options.note: Verse 19 explicitly states she is unclean for seven days.

quiz.q: What was God's stated purpose for these laws, according to verse 31?

options.text: To keep Israel separate from uncleanness so they would not die by defiling the tabernacle among them.
options.note: Verse 31 states this explicitly.

options.text: To punish Israel for committing sin.
options.note: The chapter addresses ordinary bodily conditions, not punishment for wrongdoing.

options.text: To separate Israel culturally from other nations.
options.note: True elsewhere in the law, but verse 31 specifically names defiling the tabernacle as the concern here.

options.text: No purpose is given for these laws.
options.note: Verse 31 explicitly states the purpose.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up the picture of a woman's bodily discharge from this chapter?

options.text: Jesus lets a woman with a twelve year flow of blood touch Him, and instead of becoming unclean, He heals her.
options.note: Mark 5:25-34 and Luke 8:43-48 record this directly.

options.text: The New Testament simply abolishes any concept of purity whatsoever.
options.note: This overstates the point; the Gospels show Jesus reversing the flow of defilement in one healing, not merely erasing all purity categories.

options.text: The New Testament never refers back to this chapter.
options.note: The Gospel accounts of the woman with the flow of blood directly echo this very law.

options.text: This chapter has no connection to the Gospels at all.
options.note: See Mark 5:25-34 for a direct connection.

questions: This chapter treats ordinary, unchosen bodily events as needing careful attention before a holy God. Where do you quietly assume that only your deliberate sins matter to God, and not the frailty of your body and circumstances?
Washing and waiting until evening was a small, repeatable, everyday act of returning to cleanness. What ordinary, repeatable habits help you return to God after you sense distance from Him?
Jesus let the very woman this law separated touch Him, and He was not defiled, she was healed. Where do you need to bring your uncleanness or shame to Jesus rather than staying at a distance?

God's stated reason for these laws was so He could keep dwelling among a people prone to uncleanness. How does knowing God chooses ongoing nearness, not distance, change how you approach Him after failure?

This law made no one a permanent outsider; each uncleanness had its own ordinary path back to cleanness. Who do you know who feels permanently disqualified, and how might you extend the hope Christ offers?

translationNotes.note: Bodily discharge translates a phrase built on the Hebrew root zub or zav, describing an abnormal genital flow; the same root describes a land flowing with milk and honey, so the word itself carries no shame, only meaning to flow.
Menstruation translates niddah, a word that later expands in the prophets into a broader picture of impurity and moral defilement, for example Ezekiel 36:17.

Defiling My tabernacle uses mishkan, dwelling place, the same root that names the tabernacle throughout Exodus; the concern is not abstract ritual but the actual nearness of God's presence in the camp.
